description:
Write the runtime threat list decided in "Which open runtime issues are safety gaps?" (defk-dtw.12) and give every entry a test. The list sits next to the runtime-contract table in docs/verdict.md; a safety gap is any way that code which compiles, called with any arguments, can crash the VM, corrupt memory, leak memory permanently, or break cleanup on process death or hot upgrade.

Entries (each a test):
- sizes and indices at their extremes (alloc lengths near 2^61/2^63, negative, index -1 and len)
- a yield with small heap-binary inputs (<= 64 bytes) and a forced GC between steps (reviewed safe: inputs are re-bound from the rescheduled argv on every resume)
- process killed at a safepoint (frames_live back to 0; already tested)
- a raise after alloc frees every owned buffer (reviewed safe: defk_finish on the error path)
- hot upgrade and purge mid-kernel (upgrade_test.exs)
- concurrent calls of the same kernel from many processes

Done when each entry has a passing test and the list is in the verdict draft.

comments.text: Per 'How are kernels checked against Elixir mode?' (defk-dtw.16): hostile-argument generators (wrong types, misaligned/sub-binaries, bad lengths) in defk-63k cover 'any arguments'; the deep run executes in a :peer node so a VM crash is a failing shrunk property. Hardening flags are measured in defk-j5n.

Finalized runtime threat list, one test per entry (all green: mix test 156 passed / 18s):

1. Sizes and indices at their extremes -> test/alloc_test.exs: "lengths just over the limit", "just over the macOS allocation limit (mmap tops out under 2^47 bytes)", "negative lengths", "the ticket's repro raises instead of crashing the VM", plus new "index -1 and index == len raise Enum.OutOfBoundsError in both modes" and "an index at the i64 extremes raises instead of reaching memory".
2. Yield with heap-binary inputs <= 64 bytes and a forced GC between steps -> test/heap_binary_yield_test.exs: "heap-binary inputs agree with Elixir mode while the kernel yields" and "a forced GC between two steps of a yielding kernel keeps the result correct" (a child churns its heap, starts the yielding kernel, the parent garbage-collects it while it is suspended between steps; the changed {minor_gcs, heap_size} proves the GC landed mid-kernel, and the result must equal Elixir mode).
3. Process killed at a safepoint, frames_live back to 0 -> test/upgrade_test.exs:131 "killing a kernel suspended across an upgrade frees its frame in the old library" (existing, kept: covers the harder case of a frame in the old library).
4. A raise after alloc frees every owned buffer -> test/raise_cleanup_test.exs: "a raise after alloc frees every owned buffer" (stack-frame path with a kernel that never yields, and promoted-frame path under forced yields; :erlang.memory(:binary) must come back down, ~306 MiB would be counted if defk_finish did not run).
5. Hot upgrade and purge mid-kernel -> test/upgrade_test.exs:96 "a kernel suspended across an upgrade finishes in the old library", :117 "reloading the same library while a kernel is suspended", :144 "purging the old code kills the suspended kernel, like any process in old code" (existing, kept).
6. Concurrent calls of the same kernel from many processes -> test/concurrent_test.exs: "many processes calling the same kernel at once all get the right result" (16 callers, half long enough to yield and promote, half returning within one timeslice, then the same again under forced yields; every result matches the sequential reference and frames_live returns to 0).

No safety bugs found while writing these; the existing upgrade/kill coverage (3, 5) was sufficient as written.

title: Runtime threat list with a test per entry
